fNk_zzaMoSs.summary: The first chapter of 3Blue1Brown's Essence of Linear Algebra series, introducing vectors with animated geometric visuals. It begins a series that builds intuition for linear algebra from the basics.
fNk_zzaMoSs.why: HN's go-to recommendation for learning linear algebra intuition, repeatedly credited with making concepts click and complementing textbooks.

f84n5oFoZBc.summary: Rich Hickey's philosophical talk from the first Clojure Conj in 2010. He argues that good design comes from deliberate, away-from-keyboard thinking, and describes how to feed the background mind so it solves problems.
f84n5oFoZBc.why: HN returns to it constantly as permission and method for thinking deeply before coding, and as an antidote to always-working anxiety.

fU9hR3kiOK0.summary: Martin Kleppmann argues that databases are global shared mutable state and proposes treating them as an ever-growing log of immutable facts. Derived data such as caches, indexes and views is then built by stream processors like Apache Samza. The talk draws on Kafka and LinkedIn's experience with commit logs.
fU9hR3kiOK0.why: Commenters repeatedly cite it as the talk that reframed how they think about caching, derived data and event sourcing.

f6kdp27TYZs.summary: Rob Pike's Google I/O 2012 talk shows how goroutines and channels solve tricky concurrency problems with simple Go code. It features a playful goroutine demo with gophers passing messages and a search engine example.
f6kdp27TYZs.why: The canonical recommendation for learning Go concurrency, praised as entertaining and clarifying when to use channels versus mutexes.

fKy7ljRr0AA.summary: Seven-minute footage of Fred Rogers testifying before a US Senate subcommittee in 1969 to defend federal funding for the new Corporation for Public Broadcasting. A skeptical Senator Pastore starts out abrasive and is won over during Rogers' brief, calm testimony.
fKy7ljRr0AA.why: HN commenters hold it up as a model of persuasive public speaking and as the go-to reminder of why public broadcasting deserves funding.

fD2briZ6fB0.summary: ContraPoints' 35-minute video essay on incels, examining the community, its worldview and how people get radicalized. It is delivered with theatrical style and an empathetic tone.
fD2briZ6fB0.why: Recommended as an empathetic, non-judgmental analysis of incel radicalization and how to counter it.

fHNmRkzxHWs.summary: Chandler Carruth's CppCon 2014 talk on writing fast C++, explaining why data structure choice and memory layout matter more than clever algorithms. It covers why standard containers like unordered_map perform poorly on modern CPUs.
fHNmRkzxHWs.why: A perennial recommendation for anyone learning performance optimization, cited whenever hash tables, cache behavior or STL containers come up.

fpbOEoRrHyU.summary: John Oliver's 13-minute Last Week Tonight segment explains the 2014 net neutrality fight over cable companies creating unequal internet speeds. It uses comedy to make a dull regulatory topic engaging and tells viewers how to comment to the FCC.
fpbOEoRrHyU.why: HN commenters use it as the go-to funny, accessible explanation of net neutrality and credit it with driving public comments to the FCC.

f7CW7S0zxv4.summary: Shashi Tharoor's Oxford Union speech arguing that Britain owes reparations to its former colonies, focused on the effects of British rule in India. It lists economic and political damage done by colonialism.
f7CW7S0zxv4.why: HN commenters link it repeatedly in colonial history threads as an eloquent, fact-dense short speech.

fhOHn9TClXY.summary: Joe Armstrong, creator of Erlang, interviews Alan Kay at Code Mesh. They discuss the meaning of object orientation, message passing, the META II paper, and the state of computer science.
fhOHn9TClXY.why: HN uses it in debates about what OOP originally meant, since Kay's message-passing view lines up with Erlang's processes.

fXW-QjBsruE.summary: A Vsauce video exploring whether chairs exist, through metaphysics, mereology and the philosophy of categorizing objects. It runs about 38 minutes and cites academic work on ontology.
fXW-QjBsruE.why: HN recommends it as an entertaining tour of how we define and categorize things, and it is cited when concept boundaries come up.

fE2KDzZaxvE.summary: Bryan Cantrill's Uptime 2017 talk on the engineering challenges of the stateful data path, including storage, firmware and hardware bugs. It uses the 'zebras vs. horses' diagnostic heuristic to explain why rare failures keep appearing.
fE2KDzZaxvE.why: A perennial HN favorite whenever firmware, disks, ECC or opaque hardware come up, valued as both entertaining and sobering.

f_0QlhYlS8g.summary: A 2008 Google Tech Talk in which Slava Pestov introduces Factor, a concatenative language influenced by Forth, Lisp and Smalltalk. It covers the interactive environment, metaprogramming, and the language's modern high-level features and libraries.
f_0QlhYlS8g.why: HN recommends it as the best introduction to Factor and concatenative programming, with commenters saying it impressed them with the engineering.

fbhPIK-oBvA.summary: The first part of Dmitry Vasyukov's four-part Russian documentary series about trappers and villagers living in the Siberian taiga. This episode follows spring life along the Yenisei, with hunting, fishing and subsistence in harsh surroundings.
fbhPIK-oBvA.why: Recommended as the authentic original that many prefer over Werner Herzog's shortened re-cut.

fwcl17Q0bpk.summary: Poul-Henning Kamp's FOSDEM 2014 talk is a hypothetical account of how an intelligence agency such as the NSA would sabotage open source software, standards and online discussion. It covers Skype's history, OpenSSL and psyops against standards.
fwcl17Q0bpk.why: HN returned to it repeatedly, especially after Heartbleed, as an eye-opening argument about subverting open source and standards.

f7MzFfuNOtY.summary: Real Engineering examines the efficiency of hydrogen as an energy carrier. It follows production, storage and fuel cell conversion losses and compares hydrogen cars with battery electric vehicles.
f7MzFfuNOtY.why: HN links it in hydrogen threads as a clear breakdown of why compounded inefficiencies make hydrogen a poor fit for cars, though one commenter calls it outdated.

fFSPwJFXVlw.summary: Will Wilson explains autonomous testing: using deterministic simulation and fuzzing, building on FoundationDB's approach, to test software continuously. It sets out the ideas behind his later company Antithesis.
fFSPwJFXVlw.why: HN recommends it as an excellent talk on generalizing deterministic simulation testing, and Antithesis hiring posts link it to explain the work.

f0gMdGrVteI.summary: Seeker's Focal Point short documentary on ASML's extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, which make the most advanced chips. It shows how plasma-generated 13.5 nm light is used to push Moore's Law forward.
f0gMdGrVteI.why: HN links it in semiconductor threads as an accessible overview of why EUV lithography is so hard.

ftcIcn8AmSY.summary: Guy Steele presents a small geometric problem and compares four computational approaches: a classic sequential solution and three parallel-friendly ones. Each is illustrated pictorially and with working code, weighing total work against time to solution.
ftcIcn8AmSY.why: HN points to it as a clear lesson that algebraic properties like associativity unlock parallelism, applicable in any language.

f-wWBGo6a2w.summary: Jordan Peterson's first lecture in his Biblical Series examines the idea of God as sovereignty and power abstracted from any individual ruler, and as the pattern inherent in human dominance hierarchies.
f-wWBGo6a2w.why: HN fans say it offers value even to atheists by interpreting Bible stories as psychological and evolutionary archetypes, and some credit it with helping them through depression.

fCn8zs912OE.summary: Vsauce's explainer on Zipf's law, the pattern in which the frequency of a word is inversely related to its rank. It shows the pattern across many domains and discusses why it remains unexplained.
fCn8zs912OE.why: Linked as an entertaining introduction to Zipf's law and power-law distributions.

fNpsgTIpODA.summary: Gabriella Gonzalez argues that developers misunderstand marketing as deception or hype, and applies the technology-adoption ideas of Crossing the Chasm to Haskell. She looks at what keeps Haskell from reaching mainstream programmers and what a community can do about it.
fNpsgTIpODA.why: Commenters point to it as a clear take on why functional languages stall outside niches, and its lessons are seen as applying to any technology trying to go mainstream.

fOGdb1CTu5c.summary: WIRED has UCLA professor Amit Sahai explain zero-knowledge proofs to a child, a teen, a college student, a grad student and an expert. Each round goes deeper into the cryptography and why it matters.
fOGdb1CTu5c.why: It is the go-to accessible explanation of zero-knowledge proofs, linked whenever a thread needs an intuitive introduction.

ffkIQrq-m34.summary: Bertrand Meyer's ACM webcast giving a critical look at agile methods, separating good ideas from hype and from practices he thinks damage projects. It is based on his book on the same subject.
ffkIQrq-m34.why: HN recommends it as a sober critique of agile, though one commenter found it mixed.

fwjwePe-HmA.summary: A Wendover Productions explainer on why train tickets, especially Amtrak in the US, cost so much compared with flying. It breaks down staffing, speed and the cost components behind a ticket.
fwjwePe-HmA.why: HN links it in rail-versus-air threads as a clear cost breakdown of American passenger rail.

f9EbD6iY9zI.summary: A step-by-step animated explanation of how SHA-256 works, from padding and message schedule to the compression function and final hash, with source code for the animations.
f9EbD6iY9zI.why: Commenters call it clear enough to implement the algorithm from, and teachers use it in courses.

fDqBeXJ8Zx8.summary: Coffee Break analyzes about 40,000 videos from seven months of YouTube's trending tab. It examines whether trending is biased toward mainstream media and late-night shows.
fDqBeXJ8Zx8.why: Cited in threads on YouTube algorithms and creator complaints as a data-driven look at the trending tab.

fTjhHrcyiQI.summary: A short Moneyball clip showing a manager telling a player he has been cut, directly and without softening the news.
fTjhHrcyiQI.why: HN points to it as a model for firing or laying off people clearly and respectfully.

fWqBmmPQP40.summary: Michael Steil's 27c3 talk on reverse engineering the MOS 6502 from die shots into a transistor-level simulation, as in the Visual6502 project. It covers going from chip package to a digital model.
fWqBmmPQP40.why: HN recommends it as a great walkthrough of chip reverse engineering and the story of Visual 6502.

fa28lIGuxq8.summary: Tom Scott stands by a construction site and explains why reversing vehicles now use a white-noise hiss instead of beeping. The sound is easier to locate directionally and less annoying to neighbours.
fa28lIGuxq8.why: Cited whenever backup beepers and noise come up, as a clear explanation of the white-noise alternative.

faHQA_0d9Mo.summary: A 4K AI-upscaled, subtitled fan edit of David Lynch's 1984 Dune by Spicediver that restores deleted and lost footage to form an alternative cut.
faHQA_0d9Mo.why: Recommended as the best way to watch Lynch's Dune, closer to his original vision and judged by some the best adaptation of the book.

fuFlMtZmvY0.summary: A Kurzgesagt video arguing that social media's problem is information flooding and tribal polarization. It suggests a return to smaller online communities and more in-person interaction.
fuFlMtZmvY0.why: HN recommends it in threads about dying forums and social media as a lens on why smaller communities suit us better.

f5SE47Xjx2Q.summary: PolyMatter explains China's housing bubble and why around 50 million homes sit empty. It covers cultural and economic reasons behind the overbuilding and the government's bind.
f5SE47Xjx2Q.why: Recommended as a clear, compact explainer on China's empty homes, ghost cities and property troubles.

f8ZqBLcIvw0.summary: Kraut traces centuries of political development, from Mongol rule and the Orthodox church to Muscovite autocracy, that shaped Russia's authoritarian state. It uses countryball animation and compares Russia with Europe and China.
f8ZqBLcIvw0.why: HN recommends it as a good introduction to Russian authoritarianism, though some commenters say it is flawed or wrong on many points.

fD-R35DSSZY.summary: Historia Civilis tells the story of 46 BCE, the 445-day year in which Julius Caesar reformed the Roman calendar. It covers the political context, including the civil war, Cato and Cicero.
fD-R35DSSZY.why: Recommended as an entertaining and well-explained account of why our calendar looks the way it does.

fPrvnlvnu-k.summary: An episode of This Week in Startups in which Jason Calacanis interviews Ruby on Rails creator David Heinemeier Hansson. They discuss startups, bootstrapping and 37signals' approach to business.
fPrvnlvnu-k.why: Recommended as an entertaining look at DHH's views and what the 37signals founders stand for.

fW8amMCVAJQ.summary: Derek Sivers annotates a short clip of a lone dancer at a festival, showing how a first follower turns a ridiculous act into a movement. He draws out lessons about leadership and making it easy to follow.
fW8amMCVAJQ.why: A go-to short explanation of how movements start and why early followers matter.

frLwRLS_ZR0.summary: Walt Disney Animation Studios' short introduction to path tracing, showing how rays are traced and bounced through a virtual scene to simulate light. It explains how this approach is used in animated films.
frLwRLS_ZR0.why: Recommended as an approachable intro to path tracing in ray tracing and rendering threads.

fTznEIZRkLg.summary: Hans Rosling's TED@Cannes talk uses boxes and animated data graphics to show how world population will grow to about 9 billion. He argues that raising living standards for the poorest is what reduces population growth.
fTznEIZRkLg.why: HN points to it as a data-driven, worldview-changing explanation of why global population will level off.

folTvNDL08A.summary: Physicist David Deutsch's TED talk on why science took off, arguing that good explanations are those that are hard to vary. It contrasts scientific explanation with myth.
folTvNDL08A.why: HN points to it as a short, tight introduction to Deutsch's idea of hard-to-vary explanations.

f4U8YbXKwog.summary: Micah Lee's Circle of HOPE 2018 talk on Qubes OS, which isolates activities in separate virtual machines so one compromise, such as a bad PDF or USB stick, does not expose everything. He gives an overview timed around the Qubes 4.0 release.
f4U8YbXKwog.why: Recommended as a great overview of Qubes OS and how its compartmentalization works in practice.

f8FAJXPBdOg.summary: A Capella Science parody of Ed Sheeran's Shape of You, rewritten about molecular bonding and orbitals and sung a cappella.
f8FAJXPBdOg.why: HN mentions it as an enjoyable science parody song, one of a set of A Capella Science videos.

f9vRcSAneiw.summary: Robert Smith of Rigetti Computing talks at a Bay Area Lisp and Scheme meetup about using Common Lisp for quantum computing. He covers the technical, sociological and psychological sides of working across disciplines.
f9vRcSAneiw.why: Recommended as a real-world case of Lisp in a cutting-edge industry, applied to quantum hardware.

fBt5NuNsoII.summary: A Microsoft Research talk on BetrFS, a file system built on B-epsilon trees, a write-optimized data structure. It covers WODS such as LSM-trees, how to design a file system around them, and benchmark wins over ext4 and xfs.
fBt5NuNsoII.why: HN points to it as a solid, if long, introduction to B-epsilon trees and why BetrFS is built the way it is.

fCbAafKLqC8.summary: Ben Eater explains why he builds computers on breadboards, including testing their signal behavior on an oscilloscope. It is a companion to his 6502 breadboard computer series.
fCbAafKLqC8.why: Recommended as the answer to why breadboard computers are worth building and why breadboards work at these speeds.

fHsa9DqmId8.summary: Veritasium's Derek Muller explains his hypothesis that YouTube's algorithm, not viewer preference, drives views, and that click-through rate has become the key metric. He argues this pushes creators toward clickable titles and thumbnails and leads to burnout.
fHsa9DqmId8.why: Cited in threads about recommendation algorithms and clickbait as a creator's inside view of why optimizing for click-through rate shapes content.

fPKMmJpAGWc.summary: Jose Valim introduces Nx, the project bringing numerical computing to Elixir, covering multi-dimensional tensors, automatic differentiation and JIT compilation to CPU and GPU.
fPKMmJpAGWc.why: Recommended in Elixir and machine learning threads as the introduction to what Nx makes possible.

fWDxdoRTZPc.summary: Area 5150 is a demoscene production for the original 4.77MHz IBM PC with CGA graphics and PC speaker. This is the Evoke 2022 party version, captured from real hardware, and it won the Alternative Demo compo.
fWDxdoRTZPc.why: HN treats it as a showcase of what clever tricks can squeeze out of 1981 hardware, and the sequel to 8088 MPH.

ffngZOB1U2A.summary: A /noclip documentary on GOG, covering how it finds and re-releases classic games and pushes DRM-free releases. It also touches on the company's origins in Poland.
ffngZOB1U2A.why: HN points to it as a good documentary on GOG's history and the difficulty of tracking down rights holders.

fg0_Vhldz-8.summary: A five-minute animated explainer of liquid democracy, in which voters can delegate their vote to trusted people. It starts from the origins of democracy and contrasts direct and representative models.
fg0_Vhldz-8.why: HN users share it as a brief, good introduction whenever liquid or delegative democracy comes up.

fifjjacjLBE.summary: A woodworker shows how his table saw accident happened, why it happened and how to avoid a similar one. He describes severe hand lacerations from a blade contact.
fifjjacjLBE.why: HN recommends it as a candid mea culpa and a kickback demonstration that changed how people use push blocks.

fjbWr3ODbAo.summary: Philosopher Dan Dennett argues in a TED talk that we do not understand our own consciousness and that our brains often fool us. He uses perceptual examples, including a painting that invites the viewer to fill in detail.
fjbWr3ODbAo.why: HN recommends it as a short route to Dennett's view of consciousness as a bag of tricks, often in AI and cognition threads.

fjs2gPa5sD0.summary: A clip of Jordan Peterson arguing that IQ is a strong predictor of job market success and that more complex jobs demand higher cognitive ability. He discusses what this means for people left behind.
fjs2gPa5sD0.why: HN cites it in threads on jobs, automation and hiring when arguing about IQ and employability.

fmF7HpU_-9k.summary: Felienne Hermans presents Hedy, a gradual programming language for teaching kids that moves through levels from almost no syntax toward full Python. The talk covers why error messages and syntax are scary for beginners.
fmF7HpU_-9k.why: HN points to it in beginner-programming-education threads for its distinction between easy to learn and easy to teach.

frnLiXclAMo.summary: Tom Caputi presents the design of native encryption for ZFS at the OpenZFS Developer Summit, including design decisions and how authentication uses checksum fields.
frnLiXclAMo.why: Recommended whenever ZFS encryption comes up as the authoritative explanation of how it was added and its trade-offs at scale.

fwCz8Ris79g.summary: A two-minute explanation of what a rocket mass heater is, starting from how a conventional wood stove works and why creosote and chimney fires occur. It shows how burning hot and storing the heat in thermal mass makes for an efficient heater.
fwCz8Ris79g.why: Linked as the quickest way to grasp the rocket mass heater concept in threads on heating and thermal storage.

fzBRYsiyxjI.summary: Real Engineering explains the materials science behind metal 3D printing, including crystal structure, laser sintering, and why printed parts develop fatigue cracks. It shows how process imperfections limit the strength of printed metal.
fzBRYsiyxjI.why: Commenters point to it whenever 3D-printed metal parts come up, as a clear explanation of why they have poor fatigue life and material defects.

f61KMw5zVhg.summary: A short excerpt from a BBC interview in which Richard Feynman explains why he dislikes honors and prizes, including his own Nobel, saying the real reward is the pleasure of finding things out.
f61KMw5zVhg.why: HN returns to it as a reminder to stay humble and as a source of Feynman's view on awards and prestige.

fLA_d9q6ySs.summary: Gaming Historian recounts how Atari subsidiary Tengen challenged Nintendo's licensing rules with a lawsuit and unlicensed NES games, including the lockout chip fight.
fLA_d9q6ySs.why: Recommended as a compact account of the Atari-Nintendo lawsuit and its technical and legal details, which shaped the game industry.

fQQ8IiTWHhg.summary: Numberphile with Tadashi Tokieda on the Trinity Hall Prime, a prime number whose digits form a picture of the college's coat of arms, left as a gift by a departing mathematician.
fQQ8IiTWHhg.why: Cited as the origin of the prime-number portrait trend and as an example of drawings made with primes.

f-b4QOzMyfU.summary: David Ditzel of Esperanto Technologies presents their massively parallel, energy-efficient RISC-V processors at the 7th RISC-V Workshop in 2017. It covers the high-performance many-core design aimed at machine learning.
f-b4QOzMyfU.why: Cited in RISC-V and AI hardware threads as the source for Esperanto's ambitious many-core vector design.

f1DtY42xEOI.summary: A 1969 BBC Tomorrow's World segment about Nellie, a school computer used by pupils at Forest Grammar School to solve equations and play music. Students learn programming and maintenance, and act out binary arithmetic.
f1DtY42xEOI.why: Shared as a charming historical look at children learning computing, including kids acting as register bits.

f8DQSM-b2cc.summary: Sabine Hossenfelder explains what flat earthers believe and why, arguing that their reasoning is wrong but not stupid. She suggests scientists should take such believers more seriously.
f8DQSM-b2cc.why: Pointed to in discussions about engaging with fringe beliefs and distrust of institutions rather than dismissing people.

fAxHlLK3Oyk.summary: Alvin Lucier's 1969 minimalist piece in which a spoken text is repeatedly played back and re-recorded in a room until the room's resonances replace the words. This is the 1981 Lovely Music recording.
fAxHlLK3Oyk.why: HN cites it as the canonical work behind repeated re-recording experiments, and a pivotal piece of minimalist music worth listening to patiently.

fCUTX1jurJ4.summary: A Philosophy Tube video essay on data, surveillance and the algorithms built on personal information, touching on Cambridge Analytica and the 'nothing to hide' argument.
fCUTX1jurJ4.why: Cited in privacy and surveillance threads as a thoughtful treatment of being compelled to share data and the nothing-to-hide argument.

fCd6B5HRaZ8.summary: Illumina's 3D animation of its sequencing-by-synthesis workflow, from sample preparation and cluster generation to sequencing on a flow cell and data analysis.
fCd6B5HRaZ8.why: Commenters call it the best visualization of how the most common DNA sequencers work, though it predates newer chemistry.

fHMoDt3nSHs.summary: Comedian Steve Hughes delivers a stand-up bit on political correctness, offense and health and safety culture, arguing there is no right not to be offended.
fHMoDt3nSHs.why: Cited in free speech and moderation threads as the famous comedic rant on being offended.

fKSSY1gzCEs.summary: Big Clive tears down a cheap eBay digital caliper, explaining its capacitive linear encoder and measuring its quiescent current. He finds it surprisingly accurate and repeatable for its price.
fKSSY1gzCEs.why: Cited in caliper threads as a teardown showing how cheap digital calipers work and that they are better than expected.

fPF4fBGNK0U.summary: A Consumer Reports and IIHS crash test pitting a 2009 Chevy Malibu against a 1959 Bel Air. It shows how much better modern cars protect occupants.
fPF4fBGNK0U.why: HN uses it as shorthand for how compounding engineering improvements, crumple zones especially, made things safer, applied to analogies well beyond cars.

fQqv0v14KKY.summary: A DeepSec 2010 conference talk by Ralf Philipp Weinmann on attacking the baseband processor of mobile phones rather than the application processor. It covers how open-source GSM base stations make malicious-tower attacks practical against neglected GSM stacks.
fQqv0v14KKY.why: Cited as the reference for baseband compromise, especially the point that owning the baseband can expose the application processor's memory.

fRMMSyCcTDI.summary: A hobbyist build-and-experiment video on rotating detonation engines (RDEs), where a continuous detonation wave spins around an annular chamber. The creator 3D prints parts and tests a small engine, while being candid about uncertainty over whether a true rotating wave was achieved.
fRMMSyCcTDI.why: Cited as an approachable hobbyist look at RDEs in threads on detonation-powered rockets.

fS4X1JfX6_Q.summary: Tom Scott makes a short descriptivist argument that language keeps changing and that casual internet writing conventions, like lowercase typing and dropped full stops, are legitimate. It is part of his Language Files series, written with Gretchen McCulloch.
fS4X1JfX6_Q.why: HN commenters cite it in discussions of punctuation, tone and emoji in chat as a short intro to how internet writing norms developed.

fT4lDU-QLUY.summary: Six minutes of street scenes from New York City in 1993, captured from a D-Theater HD DVHS demo tape that reused footage shot for the Japanese HiVision market. It shows Times Square and other sights in high-definition video.
fT4lDU-QLUY.why: Pointed to as striking proof of how good 1990s HD video could look, and as a window into early-90s New York.

fTTno8D-b2E.summary: A Vox report on El Paquete Semanal, the weekly offline bundle of shows, music and news that is smuggled and sold in Cuba. It shows how people get media without internet access.
fTTno8D-b2E.why: HN uses it as the standard example of sneakernet media distribution via hard drives.

fbTrLyqL_nw.summary: A Milwaukee vlogger follows teenagers known as the Kia Boys who steal Kia and Hyundai cars after a security flaw went viral on social media. The film includes interviews with participants.
fbTrLyqL_nw.why: It is cited as a firsthand look at the Kia and Hyundai theft wave, usually in threads about car security and juvenile crime.

fiD24uEvY1U.summary: RealLifeLore explains France's military posture towards Russia, including French involvement in Africa and Russian influence in the Sahel. It covers the geopolitics behind current tensions.
fiD24uEvY1U.why: Recommended as useful background on Russia's growing influence in West Africa and France's role there.

fkUwXenBokU.summary: The 1972 documentary based on Alvin Toffler's book Future Shock, narrated by Orson Welles. It is a dystopian look at the accelerating pace of technological change and its psychological toll.
fkUwXenBokU.why: Recommended as a period piece whose worries about rapid change still feel relevant to current tech anxieties.

fl4aZ2KXBsQ.summary: Adam Tornhill's GOTO Copenhagen 2019 talk on how to prioritize technical debt in large codebases. It argues for combining code complexity with change frequency (hotspots) from version control data, rather than trying to quantify debt in the abstract.
fl4aZ2KXBsQ.why: Cited as a practical approach to finding the technical debt that matters, and as a reference for codebase visualization.

fnUc_W3xE1w.summary: A lecture from the 1980s by linguist Stephen Krashen on how people acquire language. He explains his comprehensible input hypothesis for second-language acquisition.
fnUc_W3xE1w.why: HN language learners cite it as the source of the comprehensible input idea and apply it to vocabulary tools and other learning.

fo_eZuOTBNc.summary: Denis Shiryaev's neural-network-upscaled, colorized 60 fps version of film footage shot in Paris between 1896 and 1900.
fo_eZuOTBNc.why: HN cites it for the look of pre-car city streets, with pedestrians moving freely among carriages, and as an example of AI film restoration.

frAEmhqdLFs.summary: Tom Lehrer's gallows-humor song about nuclear annihilation, in which everyone goes together when the bomb drops.
frAEmhqdLFs.why: Mostly quoted as a joke in nuclear war and doom threads, with one commenter praising Lehrer's satire.

frjaQ17yAww.summary: A Jimmy Kimmel segment in which interviewers at SXSW ask festival-goers about made-up bands, and many people confidently claim to know and like them.
frjaQ17yAww.why: Used as an illustration of the confident-idiot effect and of people pretending to know things.

fsi0aJ9yr2o.summary: The original 2012 screencast introducing Meteor, a JavaScript framework for building web apps quickly. It demonstrates realtime updates, latency compensation and low boilerplate.
fsi0aJ9yr2o.why: HN remembers it as a great dev tool pitch, with commenters crediting it for showing optimistic UI and winning them over to Meteor.

fu3ETgAvQrw.summary: Neil Cicierega's parody song 'Redesign Your Logo', played over a live backing video with corporate PowerPoint visuals. It mocks the infamous Pepsi design strategy presentation.
fu3ETgAvQrw.why: Shared as a funny companion to logo-redesign and branding stories.

fxbCHn6gE3U.summary: Adam Grant's TED talk on the habits of original thinkers, including procrastination and embracing failure. He argues the greatest originals fail the most because they try the most.
fxbCHn6gE3U.why: Mentioned when discussing how to become more creative and why non-conformists are undervalued.

f1Zvo8N3G94.summary: BBC Newsnight's exclusive interview with journalist Glenn Greenwald about Edward Snowden, the PRISM revelations, and mass surveillance by the NSA and GCHQ.
f1Zvo8N3G94.why: Mostly cited as a reference to Greenwald's statements, such as his comments on press freedom, rather than recommended outright.

f1ab6uxg908.summary: A short 2019 montage of news clips about the Trump-Russia investigation, with the title ending in 'no collusion'. The channel gives no description.
f1ab6uxg908.why: Used by commenters as an example of coordinated media narratives and repeated talking points.

f3PJF0YE-x4.summary: A Chris Rock stand-up routine from Bring the Pain (1996) distinguishing between two groups of people, built around a controversial word.
f3PJF0YE-x4.why: Referenced as a well-known routine when threads discuss offensive words and who gets to use them.

f3lUEnMaiAU.summary: Alibaba's Jack Ma and Tesla's Elon Musk debate artificial intelligence on stage in Shanghai in 2019.
f3lUEnMaiAU.why: HN mostly cites it critically, as an example of Jack Ma speaking poorly or naively about machine learning.

fMeH7wqOwXA.summary: Greg Kroah-Hartman's Linaro keynote on contributing to the Linux kernel, explaining why maintainers prefer upstreamed code and how they view contributions.
fMeH7wqOwXA.why: Cited in discussions of maintainer burden and why companies benefit from upstreaming drivers, as an explanation straight from a lead kernel maintainer.

fNgEG5rCav4.summary: A TechCrunch interview with Anthony Levandowski about his new startup Pronto.ai and autonomous vehicles, after the Uber and Waymo lawsuit. He discusses lessons learned and the role of lidar.
fNgEG5rCav4.why: Cited as the source of Levandowski's remark agreeing with Elon Musk that lidar is a crutch.

f_SwD7RveNE.summary: A TiVo-captured clip of the notoriously repetitive 2006 Head On headache remedy commercial, with its 'apply directly to the forehead' jingle.
f_SwD7RveNE.why: Used purely as a joke or meme reference whenever a thread mentions heads, or repetitive ads.

fcIMIyQnOso.summary: A short clip from the movie Office Space in which a character insists he has people skills.
fcIMIyQnOso.why: Quoted as a joke in threads about engineers, dev advocates and job hunting.

fjsSr3z5nVk.summary: A two-minute clip of the printer-smashing scene from the film Office Space, set to its rap soundtrack. The uploader assembled it as a cleaner version.
fjsSr3z5nVk.why: HN mentions it only as a joke or shorthand for the urge to destroy a frustrating printer or device.

flLoSxd2nNY.summary: A one-minute clip from the film Elysium in which Matt Damon's character is stuck with an automated AI parole officer and gets asked whether he would like to talk to a human.
flLoSxd2nNY.why: Invoked as a movie reference for frustrating AI support bots and for AI that reads human emotions.

fmO-ziHU_D8.summary: A short clip from the 2014 college debate championship, posted by a commentator who criticizes the winning performance as not being a real debate. It shows a fast, unconventional style of competitive debate.
fmO-ziHU_D8.why: Used as a cited example in threads criticizing the direction of competitive school and college debate.

fn3KWM1kuAw.summary: Boston Dynamics' New Year video shows its Atlas, Spot and Handle robots dancing to 'Do You Love Me?'. It showcases the company's progress in legged dynamic balance.
fn3KWM1kuAw.why: Used as a benchmark for robot agility, with debate over how much was choreographed or real-time.

fq0RAjJ1PKQ.summary: Kyle Conner of Out of Spec Reviews finds that new Electrify America chargers co-developed with BTC fail in cold weather, then checks ChargePoint, EVgo and other EA stations during a cold snap.
fq0RAjJ1PKQ.why: Cited in EV threads as evidence that public fast-charging reliability suffers in cold temperatures.

fqYyxvM85zU.summary: A short sketch from That Mitchell and Webb Sound, the BBC radio comedy, about a safety measure that works perfectly and so gets no credit for the lack of disasters.
fqYyxvM85zU.why: It is used as a joke or shorthand for the prevention paradox, where successful safety work looks unnecessary because nothing bad happens.

fs-YpQj88ew.summary: A 1995 Letterman appearance in which Bill Gates explains the origins of Microsoft and tries to convince Dave to get a computer and get online.
fs-YpQj88ew.why: It is mostly linked as a joke or period piece about how the internet was viewed in the 1990s, not recommended for content.

ftLzQefpBvM.summary: CNN footage of correspondent Omar Jimenez and his crew being arrested live on air by police while covering protests in Minneapolis in 2020, after identifying themselves as press.
ftLzQefpBvM.why: Cited as the prime example of journalists being arrested while reporting during the 2020 protests.

fxMKuv0A6z4.summary: Penn and Teller help Rob Pike and Dennis Ritchie of Bell Labs play a prank on Nobel-winning physicist Arno Penzias. The clip shows the gag and its setup.
fxMKuv0A6z4.why: It is passed around as a favorite bit of computing folklore, and resurfaces in threads about Penzias, Ritchie and Pike.
